h1: Starting a winery: the business decisions before the vines
title: Starting a Winery: The Decisions First | Craft Beer School
desc: The business decisions to make before you plant vines or buy tanks: fruit source, scale, cash, licences, route to market and who makes the wine.
teaser: Good wine is not enough. The decisions that matter come before the first crush.
standfirst: Starting a winery is a business built around a slow, seasonal and cash-hungry product. This guide sets out the decisions to make first and the order that saves the most money.
sections: Decide the business, then test it

A winery can be a farm, a factory, a restaurant, a tourism venture or a brand. Each has different costs and a different customer. Founders who skip this choice end up buying equipment for one business and a building for another.

Write one sentence that names your customer, your price band and how the bottle reaches them. If you cannot, the rest of the plan is guesswork.

Before you sign a lease or order a press, put real wine in front of the people you hope will buy it. Buy a few bottles in your target style and price band and taste them with shop buyers, restaurant managers and likely customers. Ask what they would pay and what would make them switch.

The answer shapes everything else: price, style, bottle, label and channel. A winery that discovers this after the first vintage has already spent the money.

Wine is made once a year from fruit that will not wait. Whether you grow, buy or contract the grapes decides your land, labour, capital and risk. We cover it in detail in buying grapes or growing your own.

Vines planted today give a useful crop only after several seasons, so a grower's winery carries years of cost before the first sale. Buying fruit gets you to the first bottle sooner but ties you to someone else's quality and price.

A small winery needs more skills than founders expect. Someone must run the cellar and the lab, someone must handle sales and someone must manage licences, books and compliance. In the first years one or two people often cover several of these. The risk is that the work nobody enjoys gets skipped.

List the jobs, name the person for each and mark the gaps. A gap can be filled by hiring, by a consultant or by a partner. Cellar hygiene matters more than most beginners think, because a clean winery is the cheapest quality system you will ever own. Our guide on cellar hygiene in a small winery sets out the habits.

Good winemaking is a skill and a first vintage is an expensive place to learn it. Many new wineries hire an experienced winemaker or a consultant for the first seasons while their own team learns. Think about this before you order equipment, since the person who runs the cellar should help choose it.
Scale: start smaller than you want

A first vintage is a learning exercise that you also sell. Tanks are cheaper to add than to sell. A half-empty cellar still has to be cooled, cleaned and insured. Plan the first vintage around what you are confident you can sell within a year, then add capacity with evidence.

The cost of making a bottle falls as volume rises, but only if you can sell the extra bottles. Volume you cannot sell is stock that ties up cash.
Cash, ageing and the long wait

Red wine usually spends months in tank and often oak before release. Even a simple white sits through fermentation, settling, stabilising and bottling. Money goes out at harvest and comes back much later. Our guide on why ageing ties up money shows how to plan for the gap.

A sound plan funds the full cycle from picking to payment, with a reserve for the vintage that goes wrong.
Licences and the route to market

Alcohol is regulated everywhere. In India it is a state subject, so licences, excise and some label rules differ from state to state and they change. Rules in other countries differ too. Start the licensing conversation early with the regulator or a licensing adviser, because premises approvals can take longer than construction.

Then decide how you will sell: tasting room, shops and restaurants, a club, online where the law allows or export. Most small wineries use a mix. Each channel gives a different margin.

1. Define the business, customer and price band.
  2. Test the market with real buyers.
  3. Choose the fruit source.
  4. Draft the numbers and a business plan.
  5. Start licensing.
  6. Choose equipment and a winemaker.
  7. Fund the whole cycle, not just the building.

Each step can change the one before it, so expect to loop back. That is cheaper on paper than on a building site.
faqs: How much money does a winery need to start?

It depends on land, scale, equipment and whether you grow fruit. Work it out from your own plan: build costs, working capital for the first full cycle and a reserve. Be wary of any single figure quoted without those assumptions.
Do I need my own vineyard?
No. Many wineries buy grapes or juice from growers. Owning vines gives control but adds years of cost and farming risk.
How long before a winery earns money?
Longer than most founders expect, because wine is made once a year and often aged before sale. A fruit wine or an early-release white shortens the wait.
If you have not made wine commercially, yes, at least as a consultant for the first vintages.
